lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月5日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 精 — 音読み: セイ、ショウ / 訓読み: （常用の訓読みなし） — refined, polished; essence. This is the kanji for polishing rice itself, as in 精米（せいまい）, and the grade system is built on how far the rice is milled.
  • 磨 — 音読み: マ / 訓読み: みが-く — to polish, to grind. Brewers talk about rice being 磨（みが）かれた, "polished down," and it shows up in product names too, e.g. 獺祭 磨き二割三分（みがきにわりさんぶ）.

ことば

  • 酒造好適米（しゅぞうこうてきまい） — rice suited to sake brewing, or "sake rice." This is the formal term for varieties like 山田錦（やまだにしき） and 五百万石（ごひゃくまんごく）, which have larger grains, less protein, and usually a pronounced core. People often shorten it to 酒米（さかまい）.
  • 精米歩合（せいまいぶあい） — polishing ratio. It's the percentage of the grain that remains, not what's removed: 60% means 40% was milled away. It's printed on labels and is one of the bases of the 特定名称酒 grades.
  • 心白（しんぱく） — the opaque, starchy white core at the center of a sake-rice grain. Its starch is loosely packed, so kōji mold can grow into it easily. That's why a large, centered 心白 is prized and is what polishing aims to leave behind.
  • 精米機（せいまいき） — rice-polishing machine. For sake this usually means a vertical mill, 縦型精米機（たてがたせいまいき）, which grinds slowly so the grains don't overheat or crack.

例文

心白（しんぱく）の大きな酒造好適米（しゅぞうこうてきまい）を精米機でじっくり磨き、精米歩合五十パーセントに仕上げた。

We slowly polished sake rice with a large starchy core in the polishing machine, taking it down to a 50% polishing ratio.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月6日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 糠 — 音読み: コウ / 訓読み: ぬか — rice bran. Everything the 精米機 grinds away becomes 糠. The outer layers are 赤糠（あかぬか）, used for feed and ぬか漬け. The inner, paler layers are 白糠（しろぬか）, sold as rice flour for 煎餅（せんべい） and sweets. Its fats and proteins are exactly what brewers want gone from the grain.
  • 浸 — 音読み: シン / 訓読み: ひた-す、ひた-る — to soak, steep. This is the kanji behind the water-uptake step before steaming, 浸漬（しんせき）.

ことば

  • 枯（か）らし — the rest after polishing. Milling heats and dries the grain, so the rice is left for a few weeks to cool and draw moisture back from the air. Skip this step and the grains crack when they hit water.
  • 洗米（せんまい） — washing the polished rice to strip off the remaining 糠 powder. For 吟醸 rice it's done in small batches and quickly, because the grain starts drinking water the moment it's wet.
  • 浸漬（しんせき） — soaking the washed rice before steaming. Breweries say しんせき, dictionaries also list しんし, and you'll hear both.
  • 限定吸水（げんていきゅうすい） — timed, limited soaking. Highly polished rice absorbs water fast, so it's soaked by stopwatch, sometimes for only seconds or minutes, and weighed to hit a target uptake, often around 30%. It's a hallmark of careful 吟醸 work.

例文

精米を終えた米は二週間ほど枯（か）らしてから洗米し、ストップウォッチを片手に限定吸水で浸漬（しんせき）する。

After polishing, the rice rests for about two weeks. Then it is washed and soaked using limited water absorption, stopwatch in hand.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月7日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 蒸 — 音読み: ジョウ / 訓読み: む-す、む-れる、む-らす — to steam. Sake rice is steamed, not boiled. Steaming softens the starch so kōji and enzymes can work on it, while each grain stays separate and fairly dry. Common sake word: 蒸米（むしまい）.
  • 甑 — 音読み: ソウ / 訓読み: こしき — the traditional rice-steaming vessel, set over a big iron cauldron called a 和釜（わがま）. Outside the kura you rarely see it, but it lives on in the word 甑倒し（こしきだおし）.

ことば

  • 蒸米（むしまい） — steamed rice for brewing. All of the rice used in brewing starts out as 蒸米, whether it goes to the kōji, the starter, or the additions to the mash. Each morning the brewers check it by hand.
  • 外硬内軟（がいこうないなん） — "firm outside, soft inside," the classic goal for steamed rice. A dry, firm surface lets kōji mold grow into the grain instead of leaving it sticky.
  • 放冷（ほうれい） — cooling the steamed rice to its target temperature, either spread out on cloths or run through a 放冷機（ほうれいき）. Rice headed for the kōji room is kept warmer than rice going straight into the tank.
  • 甑倒し（こしきだおし） — literally "toppling the koshiki." It's the last steaming of the season, after which the steamer isn't needed. Kura usually celebrate with a small gathering, since it means the hardest part of the brewing season is over.

例文

外硬内軟に仕上がった蒸米を放冷し、麹室（こうじむろ）へ運ぶ。今季もようやく甑倒しを迎えた。

The steamed rice comes out firm outside and soft inside, gets cooled, and is carried to the kōji room. This season, too, we've finally reached the last steaming.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月8日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 釜 — 音読み: フ / 訓読み: かま — cauldron, kettle; it boils the water under the 甑 that makes the steam. Common sake word: 和釜（わがま）.
  • 捻 — 音読み: ネン / 訓読み: ひね-る — to twist, to pinch; this is the hand check brewers give freshly steamed rice. Common sake word: 捻り餅（ひねりもち）.

ことば

  • 和釜（わがま） — the traditional cauldron set beneath the 甑. Many kura still prize it, and its steam is often described as drier and stronger than boiler steam.
  • 連続蒸米機（れんぞくじょうまいき） — continuous steamer: rice rides a mesh belt through a steam tunnel. It's common at larger breweries. Note that 蒸 is read じょう here.
  • 捻り餅（ひねりもち） — a pinch of steamed rice kneaded and pressed flat between the fingers to judge its elasticity and stickiness, that is, whether it reached 外硬内軟.
  • 掛米（かけまい） — steamed rice added straight into the moromi during the additions, as opposed to rice made into kōji. It's the bulk of the rice in a batch.

例文

和釜（わがま）で蒸し上げた掛米（かけまい）を少し取り、捻り餅（ひねりもち）にして蒸し具合を確かめる。

They take a little of the mash-addition rice steamed over the traditional cauldron, pinch and knead it into a small flat cake, and check how well it's steamed.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月9日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 麹 — 音読み: キク / 訓読み: こうじ — kōji: steamed rice grown through with mold. It's the heart of the craft, and the brewery saying goes 一麹、二酛、三造り（いちこうじ、にもと、さんづくり）: kōji first, the starter second, the mash third. Seen in 麹米（こうじまい）, the share of rice that becomes kōji. You'll also meet the native-Japanese character 糀（こうじ） on some labels and kōji products.
  • 室 — 音読み: シツ / 訓読み: むろ — room, chamber; specifically a warm, sealed room. In the kura it nearly always means the kōji room. The word: 麹室.

ことば

  • 麹室（こうじむろ） — the kōji room: an insulated, warm, humid room, traditionally lined with cedar, where the kōji is grown over about two days. Brewers often just call it 室.
  • 種麹（たねこうじ） — kōji starter: dried spores of 麹菌（こうじきん） (Aspergillus oryzae). Kura buy it from specialist suppliers called 種麹屋（たねこうじや）, and only a handful of these remain in Japan.
  • 引き込み（ひきこみ） — carrying the cooled steamed rice into the 麹室. This is the first step of 製麹（せいぎく）, kōji-making. The rice is spread on a cloth-covered bed (床（とこ）) to even out its temperature.
  • 種切り（たねきり） — sprinkling the 種麹 over the steamed rice. It's done from a small sieve-like shaker, high above the rice so the spores fall as a fine, even dusting.

例文

引き込みを終えた蒸米を床に広げ、温度が落ち着いたところで種切りをする。麹室の中は、むっとするほど暖かい。

Once the steamed rice has been brought in, it's spread on the bed, and when its temperature has settled, the kōji spores are sprinkled on. Inside the kōji room it's stiflingly warm.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月10日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 床 — 音読み: ショウ / 訓読み: とこ、ゆか — bed, floor. In the 麹室 it's the long wooden work table where the rice is spread, spored, and kneaded. You'll see it in 床もみ and 麹床（こうじどこ）.
  • 盛 — 音読み: セイ、ジョウ / 訓読み: も-る、さか-る、さか-ん — to heap up or pile, as when serving food; also "to flourish." In the kōji room, 盛り is the step where the rice gets heaped into smaller containers.

ことば

  • 床もみ（とこもみ） — rubbing the spores into the rice on the table right after 種切り. It's done by hand so every grain is coated evenly. The rice is then piled and wrapped in cloth to hold its warmth. Also written 床揉み.
  • 切り返し（きりかえし） — roughly half a day later, the rice has warmed and clumped together. The team unwraps it, breaks up the clumps, evens out temperature and moisture, and wraps it again.
  • 盛り（もり） — once the mold is growing hard and producing its own heat, the rice is split into smaller portions (trays, boxes, or a bed) so the brewers can control heat and drying. 仲仕事（なかしごと） and 仕舞仕事（しまいしごと） follow from here.
  • 麹蓋（こうじぶた） — the small, shallow cedar tray used in the most traditional method, 麹蓋法（こうじぶたほう）. It's labor-intensive, so many kura use larger 箱（はこ） boxes or machines instead. When a label or tech sheet mentions 蓋麹（ふたこうじ）, it signals that hands-on approach.

例文

切り返しを終えた麹は、翌日（よくじつ）の盛りで麹蓋に小分けされ、温度を細かく管理される。

Once the clumps have been broken up and rewrapped, the kōji is divided into small cedar trays during the next day's portioning step, where its temperature is carefully controlled.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月11日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 破 — 音読み: ハ / 訓読み: やぶ-る、やぶ-れる — to break, tear. In the 麹室, mold "breaking into" the rice is written 破精（はぜ）: the white patches where 麹菌 has taken hold.
  • 突 — 音読み: トツ / 訓読み: つ-く — to thrust, pierce. It gives its name to 突き破精, koji whose mold pierces deep into the grain.

ことば

  • 仕舞仕事（しまいしごと） — the final round of work on the koji, roughly 30-odd hours in. The koji is spread thinner and furrowed to shed heat and moisture. It follows 仲仕事（なかしごと）, the middle round.
  • 出麹（でこうじ） — taking the finished koji out of the room, about two days after 引き込み. The word also means the finished koji itself.
  • 破精込み（はぜこみ） — how deeply the mold has penetrated into the grain. Brewers judge koji on this as much as on how much surface it covers.
  • 突き破精（つきはぜ） — koji with mold in scattered spots on the surface but reaching deep inside. Its moderate, steady enzyme power makes it the classic koji for 吟醸.
  • 総破精（そうはぜ） — koji with mold covering the whole grain and penetrating deeply. Its strong enzymes give fuller, richer sake, and it is often used for 酒母.

例文

吟醸用の麹は突き破精を目指し、仕舞仕事のあと、破精込みを確かめてから出麹する。

For ginjo koji, the brewer aims for mold that grows in spots but runs deep. After the final round of koji-room work, they check how far the mold has penetrated, then take the finished koji out of the room.

  出麹（でこうじ） — taking the finished koji out of the room, about two days after 引き込み. The word also means the finished koji itself.
  破精込み（はぜこみ） — how deeply the mold has penetrated into the grain. Brewers judge koji on this as much as on how much surface it covers.
  突き破精（つきはぜ） — koji with mold in scattered spots on the surface but reaching deep inside. Its moderate, steady enzyme power makes it the classic koji for 吟醸.
  総破精（そうはぜ） — koji with mold covering the whole grain and penetrating deeply. Its strong enzymes give fuller, richer sake, and it is often used for 酒母.
  例文  
吟醸用の麹は突き破精を目指し、仕舞仕事のあと、破精込みを確かめてから出麹する。
  For ginjo koji, the brewer aims for mold that grows in spots but runs deep. After the final round of koji room work, they check how far the mold has penetrated, then take the finished koji out of the room.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月12日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 酛 — 音読み: — / 訓読み: もと — yeast starter. A 国字（こくじ）, a character made in Japan, with no on-reading: 酉 (the wine jar) plus 元 (origin). You'll meet it in every starter method's name: 生酛, 山廃酛, 速醸酛.
  • 酵 — 音読み: コウ / 訓読み: — — fermentation, leaven. The heart of 発酵（はっこう）, fermentation, and of 酵母, the yeast that turns sugar into alcohol.

ことば

  • 酒母（しゅぼ） — the yeast starter: a small, dense batch of koji, steamed rice and water in which a large, healthy yeast population is grown before the main mash. 酒母 is the formal term; 酛 is the older brewer's word for the same thing.
  • 酵母（こうぼ） — yeast. Chosen strains (often the numbered 協会酵母 distributed by the Brewing Society of Japan) shape a sake's aroma as much as almost any other choice in the kura.
  • 乳酸（にゅうさん） — lactic acid. The starter must be acidic to keep wild yeasts and bacteria out while the sake yeast multiplies; how that acid gets there is what separates the starter methods.
  • 速醸酛（そくじょうもと） — the quick starter method: commercially made lactic acid is added at the outset instead of letting lactic bacteria produce it. Developed at the national brewing research institute around 1910, it takes about two weeks instead of roughly four, and it is used for the large majority of sake made today.

例文

速醸酛では、仕込み水（しこみみず）に乳酸を加えてから麹と蒸米を入れ、酵母を健全に増やして酒母を育てる。

In the quick starter method, lactic acid is added to the brewing water first, then the kōji and steamed rice go in, and the yeast is left to multiply healthily, raising the yeast starter.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月13日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 卸 — 音読み: シャ / 訓読み: おろす — to grind down; also to unload or sell wholesale. In the kura it lives in 山卸し, the grinding of the starter mash; on the business side you'll see it in 卸売（おろしうり）, wholesale distribution.
  • 廃 — 音読み: ハイ / 訓読み: すたれる — to abolish, discontinue, fall out of use. It gives the 山廃 starter its name ("the grinding, abolished"), and it is the 廃 of 廃業（はいぎょう）, a brewery closing its doors.

ことば

  • 生酛（きもと） — the traditional starter method: natural lactic acid bacteria from the kura environment acidify the starter over about four weeks, after the rice and kōji have been ground to a paste. Often credited with fuller, more layered, sometimes tangy sake, though the brewer's hand matters as much as the method.
  • 山卸し（やまおろし） — the grinding of rice, kōji and water into a paste with wooden poles, done in shifts in the cold. Also called 酛摺り（もとすり）. It's the backbreaking step that defines 生酛.
  • 山廃酛（やまはいもと） — the starter method that drops 山卸し: research at the national brewing institute around 1909 showed that letting the kōji's enzymes break the rice down in water does the job without grinding. It still relies on natural lactic bacteria. On labels it's usually shortened to 山廃.
  • 半切り（はんぎり） — the wide, shallow wooden tub in which a 生酛 starter is divided and ground. It's shallow so the mash stays cold and can be worked by hand; a row of them is the classic image of 山卸し.

例文

生酛では半切りに分けた酛を山卸しで摺（す）りつぶすが、山廃酛ではこの重労働を省き、麹の力に任せる。

In the traditional kimoto method, the starter is divided into shallow wooden tubs and ground to a paste with poles; the yamahai method skips this heavy labor and leaves the work to the power of the kōji.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月14日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 暖 — 音読み: ダン / 訓読み: あたたかい・あたためる — warm; to warm. In the starter room it takes the special reading だき in 暖気（だき）, the controlled warming that wakes a 生酛 or 山廃 starter up.
  • 樽 — 音読み: ソン / 訓読み: たる — cask, barrel. Familiar from 樽酒（たるざけ）, cedar-cask sake, but in the kura it also names small wooden or metal barrels used as tools, like today's 暖気樽.

ことば

  • 打瀬（うたせ） — the cold holding period in a traditional starter, after the mash is made (and, for 生酛, ground). For several days to a couple of weeks it sits at low temperature while natural lactic acid bacteria do their work, before any warming begins.
  • 暖気樽（だきだる） — a small barrel filled with hot water and lowered into the starter to raise its temperature step by step. Brewers move it in and out, and stir around it, on a careful daily schedule; today it's often stainless steel rather than wood.
  • 湧き付き（わきつき） — the moment the yeast takes over and the starter begins to ferment in earnest: bubbles, rising temperature, a fresh fermenting aroma. It's the sign that the starter is alive and on track.
  • 分け（わけ） — late in the starter's life, dividing it into smaller vessels to cool it quickly and calm the fermentation, so the yeast stays healthy until the starter is used to build the main mash.

例文

打瀬の間は酛を低温に保ち、その後、暖気樽で少しずつ温めていくと、やがて湧き付きを迎える。

During the cold holding period the starter is kept at a low temperature; then, as it is warmed little by little with a hot-water barrel, it eventually reaches the point where the yeast begins fermenting vigorously.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月15日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 醪 — 音読み: ロウ / 訓読み: もろみ — fermenting mash; the main fermentation of rice, kōji, water and yeast, built on top of the finished starter. Today we leave the 酛 behind and enter the tank: 醪（もろみ）.
  • 添 — 音読み: テン / 訓読み: そ-える、そ-う — to add, to accompany. In the kura it names each addition of rice, kōji and water to the mash, as in 初添（はつぞえ）.

ことば

  • 三段仕込み（さんだんじこみ） — three-stage mashing. Rice, kōji and water go into the tank in three batches over four days, roughly doubling the volume each time, so the yeast is never diluted faster than it can multiply and the acidity stays protective. The standard method in nearly every kura.
  • 初添（はつぞえ） — the first addition. The starter is moved to the tank and the first, smallest batch is added, kept relatively warm (around 12°C) so the yeast gets going. Often shortened to 添（そえ）.
  • 踊り（おどり） — "the dance": the rest day after 初添. Nothing is added; the yeast multiplies and the mash settles. Brewers read the mash's condition this day before going on.
  • 仲添（なかぞえ） — the second, middle addition on day three, roughly twice the first, at a lower temperature (around 9–10°C). Also just 仲（なか）.
  • 留添（とめぞえ） — the third and final addition on day four, the largest batch, mashed cold (around 7–8°C). Also 留（とめ）. After this the 醪 ferments on its own for several weeks.

例文

初添の翌日は踊りといって仕込みを休み、酵母が増えるのを待ってから仲添、留添と進めます。

The day after the first addition is the "dance" rest day: nothing new goes in, and the brewers wait for the yeast to multiply before moving on to the middle addition and then the final one.

lessons.title: 🍶 今日の酒ことば — 10月16日
lessons.html:
漢字

  • 泡 — 音読み: ホウ / 訓読み: あわ — foam, bubble; the moromi's foam rises and falls in recognizable stages, and brewers read it as a gauge of fermentation (高泡, 泡なし酵母).
  • 櫂 — 音読み: トウ / 訓読み: かい — oar, paddle; in the kura it's the long wooden pole used to stir starters and mash (櫂入れ, 櫂棒).

ことば

  • 並行複発酵（へいこうふくはっこう） — multiple parallel fermentation. Kōji enzymes turn starch into sugar while yeast turns that sugar into alcohol, both in the same tank at the same time; this is why sake can reach the high alcohol it does.
  • 櫂入れ（かいいれ） — stirring the starter or mash with the paddle. Evens out temperature, mixes rice and kōji, and feeds the yeast oxygen; how often and how hard is a brewer's judgment call.
  • 高泡（たかあわ） — the "tall foam" stage, roughly a week into the moromi, when thick foam piles up high above the mash at peak fermentation. Its height and texture tell the brewer how vigorous things are.
  • 泡消し機（あわけしき） — foam-breaker: a rotating device fitted at the tank rim that knocks down foam so it doesn't spill over. 泡なし酵母（あわなしこうぼ）, a low-foam yeast, removes much of the need for it.

例文

並行複発酵が進むと醪は高泡を迎え、蔵人（くらびと）は泡消し機を付けて櫂入れを続けた。

As the multiple parallel fermentation progressed, the moromi reached its tall-foam stage, so the brewery workers fitted a foam-breaker and kept stirring the mash with their paddles.
